text: Chapter Six Students with Asperger's Syndrome Asperger's syndrome (AS) shares some characteristics with higher-functioning autism, but also has unique features and a different developmental progression and prognosis. In British Columbia, supplemental funding designation for students with a medical diagnosis of AS should be based on the nature and extent of the disabling condition and the interventions required. These students may be reported in High Incidence categories such as "Moderate Behaviour Disorders" or "Severe Learning Disabilities," or, in a very few cases, "Severe Behaviour" or a Low Incidence category. Under DSM-IV, a child diagnosed with AS must meet the criteria for social impairment, repetitive activities, and age of onset, but have  normal cognition and early language development . AS involves fewer symptoms than autism and is considered a mild to moderate disability, while autism is usually considered severe. Learning and behavioural characteristics Social interaction People with AS may be keen to relate to others but lack the skills, and may approach others in peculiar ways. They often lack understanding of social customs, appear socially awkward, have difficulty with empathy, and misinterpret social cues. Like people with autism, they may struggle to understand that others have their own perceptions, thoughts, and feelings. They are  poor incidental social learners  and need explicit instruction. Language Children with AS usually speak fluently by Kindergarten, but often have trouble with: pragmatics  — the use of language in social contexts semantics  — multiple meanings prosody  — pitch, stress, and rhythm of speech They may have an advanced vocabulary and talk incessantly about a narrowly defined favourite subject, with difficulty switching topics. Because they don't naturally learn conversational rules, they may: interrupt or talk over others make irrelevant comments have difficulty starting and ending conversations speak with little variation in pitch, stress, and rhythm use overly pedantic or formal speech, especially in adolescence stand too close when talking stare, or use unusual posture or body language fail to understand others' gestures and facial expressions Cognition and academics Students with AS are of  average to above-average intelligence  and may appear very capable, often with extensive factual knowledge about an absorbing subject. But relative weaknesses in comprehension, abstract thought, and social cognition cause problems with: reading comprehension problem solving organizational skills concept development making inferences and judgements Thinking also tends to be rigid; they have difficulty adapting to change or failure and do not readily learn from mistakes. Motor co-ordination An estimated  50–90%  of people with AS have motor co-ordination problems — locomotion, balance, manual dexterity, handwriting, rapid movements, rhythm, and imitating movements. Sensory, attention, and anxiety Students with AS may share autism's sensory differences — hypersensitivity to some stimuli, and unusual or repetitive behaviours to obtain specific sensory input. Many are inattentive and easily distracted, and some have been diagnosed with ADHD at some point. Anxiety is also common; understanding and adapting to school's social demands can be hard, and appropriate instruction and support can relieve some of the stress. Strategies for teaching students with Asperger's syndrome Some strategies for autism apply to AS, but consider each student's unique characteristics, give support when needed, and build on their many strengths. The chart below pairs specific learning difficulties with possible classroom strategies. Learning difficulty Classroom strategies Difficulties with language makes irrelevant comments interrupts talks on one topic; talks over others difficulty understanding complex language, following directions, and words with multiple meanings use  Comic Strip Conversations  (Gray, 1994) for specific problems teach appropriate opening comments teach the student to seek help when confused teach conversation skills in small groups teach rules and cues for turn-taking, replying, interrupting, and changing topic use audio- and video-taped conversations explain metaphors and words with double meanings encourage asking for instructions to be repeated, simplified, or written down pause between instructions and check understanding limit oral questions to a manageable number watch videos to identify non-verbal expressions and their meanings Insistence on sameness prepare the student for potential change wherever possible use pictures, schedules, and social stories to signal upcoming changes Impairment in social interaction difficulty understanding rules of social interaction may be naive interprets literally what is said difficulty reading others' emotions lacks tact problems with social distance difficulty with "unwritten rules" — and once learned, may apply them rigidly lacks awareness of personal space give clear expectations and rules for behaviour explicitly teach rules of social conduct teach interaction via social stories, modelling, and role-play educate peers on how to respond use other children as cues for what to do encourage co-operative games supervise and support at breaks and recess as needed use a buddy system during unstructured times teach how to start, maintain, and end play teach flexibility, co-operation, and sharing teach self-monitoring of behaviour structured social skills groups for direct instruction and practice teach relaxation techniques; provide a quiet place model and practise appropriate personal space Restricted range of interests limit perseverative discussions and questions set firm classroom expectations, but give opportunities to pursue own interests incorporate and expand on interests in activities Poor concentration often off task distractible may be disorganized difficulty sustaining attention frequent teacher feedback and redirection break down assignments visual organizers, semantic mapping, outlining timed work sessions reduce homework seat at the front of the class non-verbal cues to get attention Poor organizational skills personal schedules and calendars lists of assignments "to do" lists and checklists pictures on containers and locker picture cues in lockers Poor motor co-ordination involve in fitness activities (may prefer these to competitive sports) account for slower writing speed — reduce assignment length extra time for tests consider a computer for written work Academic difficulties usually average to above-average intelligence good recall of facts difficulty with problem solving, comprehension, abstract concepts often strong word recognition and early reading, but weak comprehension may do well at math facts, but not problem solving don't assume understanding because the student can re-state information be as concrete as possible with new and abstract concepts use activity-based learning use graphic organizers (semantic maps, webs) break tasks into smaller steps or present differently direct instruction plus modelling show examples of what's required use outlines for note-taking and organizing avoid verbal overload capitalize on strengths (e.g., memory) check reading comprehension; supplement with visual supports Emotional vulnerability may struggle with social and emotional demands of school easily stressed by inflexibility prone to anxiety often low self-esteem difficulty tolerating mistakes may be prone to depression may have rage reactions and temper outbursts give positive praise — tell the student what they do right teach the student to ask for help teach coping and stress techniques, such as relaxation use rehearsal strategies provide opportunities to make choices help the student understand their behaviour and others' reactions educate other students peer supports — buddy system, peer support network Sensory sensitivities most commonly sound and touch; also taste, light intensity, colours, aromas noises that may feel extremely intense: sudden, unexpected noises (phone ringing, fire alarm) high-pitched continuous noise confusing, complex, or multiple sounds (e.g., shopping centres) remember normal sensory input may feel like too much or too little keep stimulation within the student's ability to cope avoid distressing sounds when possible use music to camouflage certain sounds minimize background noise use ear plugs if noise or reaction is very extreme teach and model relaxation and diversions to reduce anxiety provide quiet time and space arrange an independent workspace free of bothersome stimuli
